details:
What does it do and how does it work?

NASA tests materials for fire safety in Earth gravity, but astronauts on the Moon and Mars will live in much weaker gravity, where flames and smoke behave differently. We built an interactive web app that lets anyone drag a gravity slider from the ISS (0 g) to Mars (0.38 g) and see what changes.

The app shows two charts: how long soot stays in the flame (residence time) and the peak amount of soot. It also shows a comparison against the microgravity case, a short note on what the result could mean for smoke detection, and a Play button that sweeps through the gravity range automatically. The numbers come from three measured points in a 2026 research paper, “Smoke-point transition under partial gravity” (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1540748926003421). The app connects them with straight lines and marks where no data exists.

What benefits does it have?

Smoke detectors and safety tests are designed on Earth, where hot air rises and carries smoke upward. In low gravity that doesn’t happen. In the data we used, the time soot stays in the flame falls by about 65% between 0 g and lunar gravity, while peak soot falls by only about 22%. Smoke does not simply scale with gravity, and that is easy to see in the app.

The app lets students, the public and non-specialists explore this without reading a technical paper. It also shows why Earth or ISS assumptions can’t just be copied to the Moon or Mars.

What is the intended impact?

We want to make a little-studied problem easy to understand: fire safety in partial gravity. NASA’s standard material flammability screening is run in Earth gravity, and research suggests some materials may behave differently in lunar or Martian gravity. We hope the app helps people see why safety tests and smoke detectors need to be checked at those gravity levels.

It is an educational tool, not a validated safety model. It does not predict alarm times, and it shows exactly where the data ends. With more data, we would like to add oxygen level and cabin pressure.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

We used Python, Streamlit (web app), Plotly (charts) and NumPy (interpolation). We prototyped in Google Colab, stored the code on GitHub and deployed it on Streamlit Community Cloud. No special hardware was needed.

We used AI tools to help: DeepSeek to brainstorm the idea, and Claude (by Anthropic) to help write, debug the code, and draft the README and this description before being modified with human touch to pursue our team's standards. The research sources are linked in the app.

How is your project creative?

Most fire research is published as dense papers and tables. We turned three crucial data points into something people can drag, play and compare, with a comparison view that makes the main finding stand out.

We also built honesty into the design. The app greys out gravity levels with no data, labels interpolated values, explains what it does not do, and keeps the Earth comparison, which comes from other experiments, separate from the measured data.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Data quality: we used published research only, kept the data set small and linked the source.
  • Honest limits: with only three points the lines are estimates, and the detector advice is a simple rule we wrote, not a tested model.
  • Earth comparison: the 1 g values we found come from different experiments (jet flames), so we show them as a separate range, not on the same scale.
  • What we left out: oxygen level, pressure, materials and cabin size matter in real fires, but we had no reliable data for them.
  • Accessibility: the app is free, runs in a browser and needs no installation.
